# Proposal

The five milestones follow a tutorial from description through checking, discovery, and review.

## Milestone 1: A minimal metadata schema

We will begin with eight required fields: identifier, title, source URL, lesson URL, engine or format, maintainer, license, and learning objectives. We will map these fields to Schema.org and the Bioschemas TrainingMaterial profile where applicable. Topic, level, prerequisites, packages, deployment mode, duration, accessibility information, and software versions will be optional in the initial schema. Optional review references and DOIs will identify external reviews and publications. The checking tools will generate validation dates and results.

To reduce manual work, we will evaluate drafting metadata from existing tutorial sources. Suggested topics, prerequisites, learning objectives, and difficulty will require human confirmation before publication. Records will distinguish author-supplied values, mechanically extracted information, and inferred suggestions, with review status recorded separately. Parsing, heuristics, or AI may assist drafting; the registry pilot will measure whether it reduces author effort.

Authors will supply missing fields in a small accompanying file without rewriting lessons. Unknown values will remain explicit, and nominations with unknown maintainers or licenses will remain pending review. Adapters will run checks only when the required information is available; unconfirmed suggestions will not establish prerequisites for a check.

We will align the prototype with this draft and invite engine maintainers and educators to review it. Their feedback and the pilot's measures of author effort will guide revisions before we publish version 1.0 with example records and adoption guidance.

## Milestone 2: Harden and extend engine adapters

The prototype implements `learnr_adapter()`, `learnr2_adapter()`, and `quarto_live_adapter()`, producing a common report through `check_tutorial()`. We will harden and extend these adapters, refine their interfaces with maintainers, and document supported versions and features. Because learnr2 and Quarto Live share formats, format detection alone cannot always distinguish them.

Adapters may invoke an engine's existing build or checking tools; the engine remains responsible for execution. Conversion between engines is outside the adapters' scope. A capability table will show each adapter's support for metadata import, rendering checks, code execution, and accessibility checks. Engines can support different checks while reporting results in the same format. Carpentries-style materials can be indexed after metadata and link checks. Further checks will depend on the lesson's build system, with those limits stated in the registry.

## Milestone 3: Validation across engines

`check_tutorial()` already combines metadata, URL, and optional rendering checks using four statuses: `pass`, `fail`, `not_run`, and `unsupported`. Grant work will add deeper engine-specific checks of required files, declared dependencies, package versions, interactive execution, and exercise identifiers where supported. Basic automated accessibility checks will accompany manual keyboard checks. Reports will distinguish observed results from declared accessibility information.

We will automate reproducible checks and investigate browser tests of representative exercises and assessments. Successful rendering will remain distinct from evidence that interactive behavior works. Reports will identify failing fields or exercises and record the test environment, source version, and date. Automated checks alone will not establish teaching quality or full accessibility.

We will publish a reusable GitHub Actions workflow and integration guidance so authors can run checks in their own repositories without joining the registry. CI will test the package on Linux, macOS, and Windows, using examples with known faults to verify that the checks detect problems. Documented real renders currently cover macOS only.

## Milestone 4: A searchable tutorial registry

The registry will link tutorial descriptions to the original repositories and published lessons. Authors will retain responsibility for content and hosting. Automated builds will use YAML entries to create the searchable website and publish `index.json`. A proposed `tutorial_search()` function will return results as an R data frame.

Readers will filter by topic, package, level, learning objective, engine, and deployment mode when those fields are available. Each entry will show duration and maintenance status when known, and distinguish metadata validity from execution checks and human review. Scheduled checks will flag broken links and outdated validation records.

The indexing pilot will cover 5–10 existing tutorials across the supported formats. We will record missing fields and manual corrections to measure author effort. Completion will require valid records and working search results; claims about execution will depend on separate adapter tests.

## Milestone 5: Review, governance, and example tutorials

Authors will submit entries through structured pull requests; others can nominate tutorials. Automated checks will precede registry review of metadata completeness, scope, licensing, maintenance information, and declared accessibility characteristics. Review procedures will draw on open lesson-review practices [@carpentrieslab2022]. Where tutorials have undergone external pedagogical or scholarly review, we will link to that review rather than repeat it. Our guidance will distinguish nominations from author submissions and explain procedures for correcting, removing, or archiving entries. It will also specify responsibility for maintaining each part of tutorialverse.

We will use four small example tutorials to test the adapters: renv, package development with usethis and devtools, an introductory DESeq2 workflow, and a Carpentries R companion. We will choose representative exercises and adapt existing material under compatible licenses. Bharti's r-for-beginners lessons and Bioconductor training resources offer starting points.

These examples will test metadata mapping, validation reports, and each engine's checks; the indexing pilot will test how existing tutorials are described and found. The four examples will collectively cover all three adapters, without requiring every tutorial to run under every engine. Tests will include browser interaction where supported and local or server execution where needed. Three or four small integration templates will show authors how to connect existing lessons through their chosen engine.
